title: What smaller banks would gain from fewer supervisory demands
summary: Frank Elderson wants to release staff time at small euro area banks without changing the safety standards applied to depositors. His proposal has two parts. Some banks with simple businesses would become eligible for the existing proportionate supervisory framework. Banks already inside it could face less duplication in reporting and stress testing. Neither change gives a bank additional capital. The argument for local credit supply runs through lower operating costs and better use of specialist staff. The contribution presents no estimate of extra lending.

The existing arrangements already have broad reach. Around 75% of the banks supervised by national authorities in the euro area, more than 1,400 institutions, qualify as small and non-complex. The share in Germany is 81%. These percentages count banks, so they say little by themselves about the share of euro area assets or loans affected. Qualifying institutions need report at most 30% of the data their larger counterparts report. Supervisors can also vary the intensity and frequency of checks with the complexity and risks of each bank. Elderson's starting point is therefore an established distinction whose current definitions leave some comparatively straightforward institutions outside it.

Germany supplies his case for changing the asset threshold. Local mergers can create a bank with more than €5 billion in assets without adding complex products or international activities. A larger regional institution may spread overheads across more customers and afford investment in digital operations and cybersecurity. Elderson favours changing the regulation so that national authorities could raise the limit to €10 billion when a bank's risk profile and the structure of its domestic market warrant it. This would give them discretion. A balance sheet below €10 billion would not automatically confer eligibility. A second change would address banks excluded by technical aspects of resolution planning. Together, the legislative changes could bring roughly 150 more banks within the framework.

A larger operational constituency is already within reach. For banks with stable, well-understood risks, supervisors could perform stress-test projections centrally. Elderson estimates this could lighten the workload of almost 1,000 institutions that currently produce projections themselves. Separately, the ECB and European Banking Authority are pursuing reporting changes that would eventually bring small banks' required data points to around 5% of those reported by large banks. The 5% figure is a prospective comparison with large institutions. It does not mean every eligible bank will cut its present reporting costs by five-sixths because the existing 30% is an upper bound and the cost per field is unknown. Nor should the estimates of 150 and 1,000 be added. They refer to different changes and may cover some of the same institutions.

The trade-off matters most where a simple business model coexists with a concentrated local risk. The same relationships that help a regional lender finance households and the Mittelstand can give local knowledge particular value in assessing borrowers. Cyber threats, geopolitical disruption and climate or nature-related damage can still affect that bank and the firms it finances. Central projections can replace repetitive modelling work, but less frequent bespoke assessment only fits Elderson's stated criterion when the risk profile remains well understood. For holders of smaller banks' debt, the information to watch is which institutions qualify, which exercises migrate to supervisors and which material local exposures remain visible afterwards. No capital relief, implementation date or assurance of margin improvement is announced in this opinion piece.

questions.question: Which institutions would gain meaningful eligibility from a national €10 billion threshold?
questions.detail: Compare the assets, product mix, cross-border activities and resolution-planning status of banks around the present €5 billion limit. Distinguish banks newly admitted by size from those admitted by revised complexity criteria. For each group, identify which reporting or supervisory work would actually disappear. This would convert the estimated 150 potential entrants into an economically relevant measure of exposure.

questions.question: Do central stress projections preserve warnings about concentrated local borrowers?
questions.detail: For banks assessed under both approaches, compare central and bank-run stress losses, especially in sectors concentrated within one region. Check where supervisors or bank staff had to override a projection, what information prompted the override, and how much work both parties performed. Large differences would help identify institutions for which a less frequent bespoke exercise remains valuable.

questions.question: Would lower reporting effort change bank economics or simply move the work?
questions.detail: Track staff hours, data-system costs and supervisory requests alongside the number of mandatory fields. Distinguish genuine savings from requests shifted into ad hoc exercises. Then test whether savings fund digital resilience, improve the cost-to-income ratio, or support additional lending to comparable local borrowers. Each outcome has different implications for bank creditors and businesses seeking finance.
